questions.q: Why does EXISTS usually perform well for a pure existence check?
options: It stops scanning the moment it finds one matching row — it never needs to know how many matches exist
It always returns fewer rows than IN or JOIN
It automatically adds DISTINCT internally
It requires an index to function at all
questions.explain: This short-circuiting behavior, from Lesson 55, is exactly why EXISTS suits presence checks.

questions.q: Why does the JOIN version of an existence check need DISTINCT?
options: A product with multiple matching order rows produces multiple joined rows, not one — DISTINCT collapses them back down
JOIN always returns fewer rows than the source table
DISTINCT is required syntax for every JOIN, regardless of the scenario
JOIN cannot be used with WHERE otherwise
questions.explain: This is the real, avoidable extra work the JOIN approach introduces compared to EXISTS/IN.

questions.q: What is the most common bug when writing a JOIN-based existence check?
options: Forgetting DISTINCT, which produces duplicate rows for products with multiple matches — a correctness bug that looks harmless
Using INNER JOIN instead of LEFT JOIN
Forgetting to alias the tables
Using WHERE instead of ON
questions.explain: The query still runs and returns plausible-looking results, making this an easy mistake to overlook.

questions.q: When should you reach for JOIN instead of EXISTS/IN for this kind of question?
options: When you need columns from the related table, not just whether a match exists
Whenever performance matters at all
JOIN should always be preferred regardless of the question being asked
Only when the related table has fewer than 100 rows
questions.explain: EXISTS/IN can only test for presence — they can't return the matched row's own data, which is exactly what JOIN is for.

questions.q: How does IN typically compare to EXISTS for a simple existence check?
options: It behaves similarly and is often optimized identically by SQL Server for this case
IN is always dramatically slower than EXISTS
IN cannot be used for existence checks at all
IN always returns duplicate rows, requiring DISTINCT
questions.explain: For this specific existence-check pattern, IN and EXISTS are close in behavior, unlike the JOIN approach which needs deduplication.
